I farm in Quzhou County, so I will keep to the cropping pattern that is the safest and most familiar for my land: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That fits our local climate, water conditions, and the way I already know how to manage fields. At my age and education level, I will not gamble on complicated cash crops that need more market timing or fine technical management. I care most about stable grain yield, manageable costs, and work I can organize with the machinery and habits I already have.

I will put most of my land into this wheat-maize rotation. For winter wheat, I will use improved seed, not old saved seed, because I want better emergence, disease resistance, and more even yield. I will till with a rotary pass after fertilizer and residue handling so I can get a clean seedbed without spending too much on deep ploughing every time. I will use moderate fertilizer, with nitrogen highest, phosphorus next, and some potassium to keep the stand strong. I will irrigate a few key times instead of too often, because water matters most at the turning points. I will spray only as needed for weeds, aphids, and disease pressure. After wheat harvest, I will move quickly into summer maize with hybrid seed because maize yield depends heavily on stand uniformity and vigor. I will keep fertilizer balanced but push nitrogen more on maize, irrigate around the key growth stages if water is available, and control weeds and insects in a timely way. This is the plan I would trust most for a steady year.
